catalog_quote: van den Berg 2009, p. 23: "5 Tone. The Awing language is a tonal language and exhibits three phonetic tone levels: low, mid and high; and two contour tones: rising and falling." ... "5.1 Automatic Downstep. High tones become phonetically lower (mid) following low or falling tones. Because surface high tones never follow a low or falling and because mid tones never appear except after a low or falling, we treat all phonetic mid tones as the result of automatic downstep from high tone." — Fominyam 2021, p. 160: "In intonation languages like English or German, focalization can be achieved, among other means via prosody; for example, by stressing the focalized word/constituent within the sentence. This is not the case in (most) tonal languages like Awing. However, there is a prosodic mechanism, namely the notion of truncation that applies in focus contexts." — p. 310: "in languages like Georgian and German, either the noun or the quantifier can be accentuated with a higher pitch accent, but such stressing rules are not applicable in a tonal language like Awing."
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (26 pp., text). Printed p. 23 (pdf page 23) §5 Tone reads verbatim: "The Awing language is a tonal language and exhibits three phonetic tone levels: low, mid and high; and two contour tones: rising and falling." §5.1 Automatic Downstep on the same page: "High tones become phonetically lower (mid) following low or falling tones.. we treat all phonetic mid tones as the result of automatic downstep from high tone." A a full-text search for stress/accent the whole sketch for stress/accent/prominence/intonation returns one hit only, p. 19 "pronounced with less emphasis" about the second C of consonant clusters; the sketch (consonants, vowels, syllable structure, tone) never mentions word…
new_statements.rule_in_words: No source states where word stress falls. Awing is described as a tone language with underlying H vs L (phonetic mid = downstepped H) plus rising and falling contours on roots; the dedicated phonological sketch (van den Berg 2009) and the orthography guide (Alomofor & Anderson 2005/2007) never mention stress or accent. The only mention of stress in any source is Fominyam's remark, in a syntax discussion, that prominence-by-stressing (pitch accent focus marking of the English/German type) is not applicable in tonal Awing; this is a statement about sentence-level focus prosody, not about word-level stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None (no stress rule given). Tone facts noted: noun-class prefixes are almost always L (a few archaic H prefixes mə́-/kə́-); consecutive verbs take an H nasal prefix; verb roots show two underlying patterns (H+HL, L+HL floating); grammatical tone marks habitual aspect.
new_statements.domain_note: van den Berg's tone data are citation (isolation) forms of single-root nouns (728) and verbs (770); orthography guide writes tone as pronounced in isolation. Fominyam's remarks concern focus marking at sentence level, where Awing uses a truncation mechanism instead of stress.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe the Awing of Awing village (Santa subdivision, Mezam division, NW Cameroon), i.e. the main Mbwe'wi variety; the Seguin & Mbongue 1994 survey concerns the Bamukumbit dialect area and has no phonology. No dialect-specific stress claims exist.

new_statements.quote: Awing is a tone language that distinguishes between high (á), low (a, unmarked), rising (ǎ) and falling (â) tones. Tones distinguish lexical and grammatical information.
new_statements.citation: Fominyam, Henry Zamchang & Doreen Georgi. 2021. Subject marking in Awing. Studies in African Linguistics 50(1): 82-115.
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File (34 pp., text; line 40 and p. 83 head) reads exactly: 'Awing is a tone language that distinguishes between high (á), low (a, unmarked), rising (ǎ) and falling (â) tones. Tones distinguish lexical and grammatical information.' The sentence spans the p. 82/83 page break in §1 Introduction, as the locator says. Independent a full-text search for stress/accent the full text for stress|accent|prominen|intonation|pitch|prosod: 'prominent' only in the sense of 'well-known analysis' (lines 244, 298, 307, 374), 'intonation break' as a topic-dislocation diagnostic (lines 983-987), 'accent' only in the bibliography title Byarushengo/Hyman/Tenenbaum 1976 on Haya. No word-stress statement. Identity…
new_statements.relation_note: Same characterisation as the existing statement (van den Berg 2009; Fominyam 2021): tonal language, four tones (H, L, rising, falling), nothing on stress. Note van den Berg 2009 counts the phonetic mid as automatic downstep of H, so 'four tones' here = the same inventory.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Syntax paper on subject markers; the only prosodic statement is a one-line note that Awing is a tone language with four tones. The words 'stress' and 'accent' do not occur in the text (only 'intonation break' as a topic-dislocation diagnostic, p. 106, and 'prominent' in the sense of 'well-known analysis'). No word-stress statement.
new_statements.identity_note: Azieshi 1993 (p. 96) treats awiŋ as the base variety of a group with ten other dialects; her data are the Awing of Bamukumbit (ALCAM 917). Fominyam & Georgi 2021 data come from the first author, a native speaker. No source names a sub-dialect for its stress/tone statements.

new_statements.quote: La langue awiŋ est une langue à ton. Chaque voyelle porte un ton, signalant ainsi un centre de syllabe. Cependant, il existe une nasale syllabique N̩ qui se comporte comme noyau de syllabe. Par conséquent, elle porte un ton qui est toujours bas. Il ressort de nos investigations les quatre tons suivants. [1.1.1 Le ton haut ... 1.1.2 Le ton bas ... 1.1.3 Le ton montant ... 1.1.4 Le ton descendant]
new_statements.translation: The Awing language is a tone language. Every vowel bears a tone, thereby signalling a syllable centre. There is however a syllabic nasal N̩ which behaves as a syllable nucleus; consequently it bears a tone, which is always low. Our investigations yield the following four tones. [1.1.1 The high tone ... 1.1.2 The low tone ... 1.1.3 The rising tone ... 1.1.4 The falling tone]

new_statements.relation_note: Confirms the tone-language characterisation with no stress statement; refines the existing statement only in giving the 1993-94 four-tone inventory (H, L, rising, falling) that van den Berg 2009 later analysed with automatic downstep. The item is the same document as index 2 (title page: 'Mémoire présenté en vue de l'obtention du DIPES II.. Année académique 1993-1994'). Opened via the PuRe REST file endpointhttps://pure.mpg.de/rest/items/item_403400_4/component/file_403399/content(file is PUBLIC; the HTML record page could not be reached by automated download bot-check)
new_statements.rule_in_words: The prosody chapter (pp. 50-54) is entirely about tone: four tones H, B, BH (rising), HB (falling), reduced to four tonemes (§1.2-1.4), with their distribution in §II.3 (pp. 60-65). Word stress/accent is never discussed; the sole occurrence of 'accent' is inside the Dubois et al. 1973 dictionary definition of tonème quoted on p. 50 ('une unité accentuelle de hauteur qui permet d'opposer deux unités significatives'). Conclusion p. 96 lists the distinctive units as 'quatre tonèmes, neuf phonèmes vocaliques, et vingt-huit phonèmes consonantiques'.
new_statements.exceptions: Syllabic nasal always carries low tone (p. 51).

[...] The Awing language is a tone language. Every vowel bears a tone, thereby signalling a syllable centre.

sources.note: §1.7 Phonology (pp. 15-17) gives segment charts and a five-tone chart taken from Alomofor et al. (2007); no word-stress statement. Two passing remarks in syntax chapters: p. 160 'focalization can be achieved.. by stressing the focalized word/constituent within the sentence. This is not the case in (most) tonal languages like Awing'; p. 310 'such stressing rules are not applicable in a tonal language like Awing'. 'Stressed pronouns' (p. 38) = strong/emphatic pronoun forms, not phonetic stress.
